answer.summary: Wes Kao recommends proactively sharing an evidence-backed point of view and recommendations, rather than making your manager solve the problem from scratch. Keep your manager informed and aligned as your plans and responsibilities evolve.

sections.heading: Bring a recommendation, not just a question
sections.content: Instead of asking only, “What should we do?”, explain what you think should happen and invite your manager to respond: where are the gaps, and are you thinking in the right direction? That gives them something concrete to build on and reduces their mental load. A weekly task recap can be useful, but Kao sees sharing your point of view as more highly leveraged.

sections.heading: Support your view with evidence and observations
sections.content: Back up your perspective with evidence, and share hypotheses or problems you have noticed—even if you do not have a perfect answer. When reporting results, point out the insights and takeaways instead of leaving all the interpretation to your manager. Kao says this demonstrates active, strategic thinking; it is something junior employees can do too, especially when they have close visibility into customers or operational issues.

sections.heading: Keep alignment ongoing
sections.content: Managing up is not something you outgrow: it continues and changes as your career progresses. Especially when work is ambiguous, keep your manager in the loop about what you are planning to try and what you are doing, and make sure you are aligned.
